titleStmt.title: Adjusting Real-Time Mode Transitions via Genetic Algorithms

analytic.title: Adjusting Real-Time Mode Transitions via Genetic Algorithms

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: The problem of mode transition schedulability of real-time systems is examined using a genetic algorithm. Due to the mode transition, there can be an overuse of the resource, i.e. the processor(s). A mode transition deadline is a time period in which the outgoing mode(s) have to finish, and then after the mode transition the resource can be completely used by the incoming mode(s).

The primary goal of this work is to formulate sensitivity analysis of mode transitions using a genetic algorithm, such that the task set parameters are changed as little as possible to meet the mode transition deadline. This work increases the periods of incoming tasks to ensure that mode change deadlines are met.

When the mode change request occurs, we have conflicting goals -start the new mode and finish the mode transition as soon as possible. If new mode tasks need to start before old mode tasks are able to complete, we need to take some corrective action. Some possibilities include : aborting old mode tasks, extending periods of new mode tasks, or reducing execution time of either old mode or new mode tasks. Our research explores the approach of increasing new mode task periods.

Earlier works used task-by-task algorithms. This is unlike the genetic algorithm approach which treats the entire task set at once. The genetic algorithm can schedule the tasks such that the mode transition deadline is met sooner than the previous techniques and with higher utilizations. Deadline increases of incoming task periods can lessen the mode transition time and improve the utilization of the resource. Rather than task by task changes of previous works, the genetic algorithm can find a global change which is smaller.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time systems have to be scheduled so that all tasks meet their deadlines. In general, the scheduling problem is co-NP hard [1]. The real-time scheduling problem has added complexity when considering the sensitivity analysis of unschedulable task sets and the schedulability of multi-mode systems.

A prototype mode transition can be described by airplane flight. A typical flight has several modes, such as take-off, cruising, and landing. The real-time system has to change the use of the resource from one set of tasks to another within a certain period of time. Potentially it is important to minimize the transition time due to instability of overloading the resource.

Modes are necessary for real-time systems which have to change the usage of the resource with ≥ 2 possibly different task sets at certain times. Modes are sets of tasks, having different functionality. There are periods of time, called mode transitions, in which 2 or more modes, with two different sets of tasks, are executing at the same time. The burden of scheduling ≥ 2 sets of tasks may cause deadlines to miss. The mode transition deadline is the time by which the mode transition should end [2].

This work presents mode transition sensitivity analysis by changing task periods. This is a generalization of sensitivity analysis problem. Mode transitions have been modeled and examined in several works [2] [3]. Several protocols have been given and are reviewed in [4]. Sensitivity analysis is defined by changing the task set parameters of an unschedulable task set into a schedulable task set. Changing the task set parameters such as periods, deadlines, and offsets, have been examined in many works, for example [5]- [10].

Mode transitions have both incoming and outgoing task sets executing at the same time; this could lead to a combined utilization greater than 100 percent. The combined task set is clearly unschedulable. The task sets have to be changed in order to make the mode transition schedulable. The mode transition ends after the outgoing tasks have completed. A mode transition deadline is potentially important due to constraints from the demands of the real-time system.

In this work, a genetic algorithm (GA) is used to find a minimal mode transition time and minimal task parameter changes that make the mode transition schedulable. The genetic algorithm can use a constraint that the mode transition completes before a mode transition deadline. Genetic algorithms have been used in the past in realtime systems, e.g. [11]. The genetic algorithm, unlike previous sensitivity analysis approaches, incorporates the minimal mode transition time limit as a constraint; this minimal time can be as small as possible due to using it in a constraint. The GA can outperform previous mode transition techniques in both minimizing the mode transition time and in minimizing task set changes. The current work shows this in the experiments and also that the utilization of the resource during the mode transition is higher as compared to known mode transition scheduling algorithms.

The genetic algorithm approach has several advantages over previous techniques. For example, previous techniques could fail to find a feasible schedule if the mode transition deadline value is less than the required time. Second, the genetic algorithm provides choices to the set of task parameter changes, unlike known techniques. The genetic algorithm is more effective and flexible as a result.

This work compares the use of the genetic algorithm in the mode transition problem to previous sensitivity analysis works, modified to the mode transition problem. To summarize these sensitivity techniques, -ScaleSA [12] scales all the periods or execution times by the same factor, until the task set is schedulable. While this approach is very quick, the resulting task sets differ widely from the original task set.

-TbTSA [6] (task-by-task sensitivity analysis) changes the task parameters from the highest priority to the lowest. In the implementation the tasks' periods are changed one at a time until schedulability is achieved. This algorithm increases the periods of lower priority tasks disproportionately. This approach also runs more slowly than scale SA and is ineffective in minimizing task set changes.

-BiniSA [10] approach uses modified TDA equations and the idea of the "feasibility region" to find an efficient dynamic programming algorithm. The feasibility region was introduced in [10] and used to find task period increases such that the schedule is feasible. This work also changes task periods task-by-task. The minor disadvantage of this approach is that initial utilization has to be less than 100 percent.

The outline of the paper is the following. Section 2 describes the model. Section 3 describes the formulation of the genetic algorithm in the context of the mode transition sensitivity analysis. Section 4 describes the experiments and the comparison of the genetic algorithm with earlier techniques. Section 5 concludes and discusses avenues of future research.

div.head: MODEL AND DEFINITIONS
div.p: Independent tasks are scheduled with rate monotonic (RM) fixed priority, pre-emptive scheduling. The priorities of tasks are set in order of increasing periods [13]. There are different modes, denoted by {M 1 , M 2 , . . . , M mmax }. There are a total set of tasks and each mode M uses a subset of the total set of tasks. These tasks are characterized by execution times e i , periods T i , and deadlines D i . These are 3-tuples {e i , T i , D i }. The incoming task τ i releases a sequence of jobs τ i,0 , τ i,1 , ... with τ i,k having release time kT i and deadline (k+1)T i . This is for the model we use in which the incoming tasks release their jobs at the mode change request instant. Each job must be allowed to execute for e i time units between its release time and deadline. We take periods equal to deadlines in our model. All periods and execution times are integers, (T i ∈ Z and e i ∈ Z). Not all tasks are in the different modes; those in all the modes are mode independent.

Define the outgoing tasks by O and the incoming tasks by I. I i is the set of incoming tasks with higher priority than task τ i , and O i is the set of outgoing tasks with higher priority. The usual time demand analysis (TDA) equations [14] for a task set using fixed priority TDA preemptive scheduling for the task set, with periods T i , execution times e i , and worst case response times w i , is
div.formula: w (k+1) i = e i + τj ∈Hi w (k) i T j e j . (2.1)
div.p: where H i is the set of higher priority tasks than task i.
As is well known, these equations are solved iteratively for each task τ i until a fixed point w
div.formula: (k+1) i = w (k) i is found with w (k) i ≤ T i , or a deadline miss is identified, w (k) i > T i .
div.p: In the case of the mode transition problem, these TDA equations have to be changed to deal with both the incoming and outgoing tasks. The priorities of the incoming and outgoing tasks are in general different. This is important, as interferences from the incoming tasks could delay the outgoing tasks' worst case response times and thus increase the mode transition time. The mode transition time is the worst case response time w l of the lowest priority outgoing task τ l , which defines the outgoing task set O completion,
div.formula: w (k+1) l = τj ∈O e j + τi∈I l w (k) l T i e i , (2.2)
div.p: where all outgoing task execution times are included. This equation finds the worst case response time of the lowest priority outgoing task. If all the incoming tasks have lower priorities than the outgoing tasks, then the mode transition time is truly minimal since there is no interference from the incoming tasks. In this case the mode transition completion is just the sum of the execution times of the outgoing tasks. If there are mixed priorities, then the mode transition time depends on the periods of the incoming tasks; this time can be lessened by increasing the periods of the incoming tasks, which in turn reduces the interference with the outgoing tasks. Figure 1 illustrates a simple mode transition and how the interference of the incoming tasks has an effect on the mode transition time. By increasing the periods of the incoming tasks, the mode transition time is decreased. The goal in this work is to use a genetic algorithm to find the minimal change in the task parameters such that the mode transition is over before a specified mode transition deadline. The algorithm is compared with earlier approaches.

div.head: GENETIC ALGORITHM
div.p: The genetic algorithm uses an inequality form of the TDA equations given above.

Because the TDA equations are discontinuous nonlinear equations over the variables w i (1 ≤ i ≤ N ), we use complex optimization strategies, such as a genetic algorithm, to find an optimal (or close to optimal) solution to the minimization of task set parameter changes. Genetic algorithms (GA) are a well-known method for optimizing complex problems using evolutionary computation.

In the TDA GA, each individual of the population is made from a set of period-scaling factors λ i of the incoming tasks and worst case response times w i of all tasks (both incoming and outgoing tasks). Each of these parameters are genes of the individual; for a transition of 2 modes, each with N/2 tasks (same size), there are 3/2N genes -namely, the N/2 scaling factors of the incoming tasks, and the N worst-case response times of both modes. There is a fitness given to each of the incoming task individuals which involve both the objective function and the constraints. The population is improved until the sum of the incoming task scaling factors is minimized. The user must specify when the algorithm will stop by providing a desired accuracy of the solution -the tolerance in both the objective function and constraints.

The genetic algorithm's search space could be quite large. For example, if period increases range from 0 to 100 and there are an incoming set of 100 tasks, then the search space is approximately 100 200 = 10 400 . This follows from the fact that there are 200 worst case response times of incoming and outgoing genes, each of which could have values from 0 to 100; if the worst case response times are larger than 100 then the search space increases. There are also 100 scaling factor genes from the incoming mode, which increases the search space. Adding the scale factors of the incoming periods increases the search space also; if the scale factors are discretized, for example, as 1.01, 1.02, ..., 2.00 then this is another 100 100 . For problems of this size, the GA could be slow, though tuning the parameters carefully can have a dramatic impact on the runtime. It is important to reduce the search space by initializing the population near a possible solution; this increases the efficiency of the GA.

The GA uses scale factors λ i to increase the periods of the incoming tasks; The incoming task periods T i are scaled by factors of λ i . If there are 2 modes, then the chromosome is defined by an ordered sequence,
with i and j labeling the tasks of the incoming and outgoing modes I and O.

An objective function and a set of constraints is required in the genetic algorithm. Due to equality constraints being difficult in a genetic algorithm, the task set TDA equations are used in an inequality form in the constraints, This objective function is used with the scale factors, not the period increases, because tasks with large periods are treated effectively the same as tasks with small periods.
div.formula: w i ≤ e i + τj ∈Ii w i λ j T j e j + τ k ∈Oi e k . (3
div.p: There is one last constraint, which demands that the mode transition is over before a period of time, defined by a multiple of the minimal mode transition time, which is τi∈O e i if no incoming task executes at all during the mode transition.

The mode transition deadline is used as a constraint in the genetic algorithm. There is no constraint in the remaining three algorithms: scaleSA, TbTSA, and BiniSA. In these cases, the schedulability of the mode transition is found, and the mode transition deadline constraint is used by further increasing the scale factors of the incoming task periods.

div.head: EXPERIMENTS
div.p: In this section, the experiments demonstrate the performance of the GA and it is compared with earlier techniques of sensitivity analysis. The Matlab global optimization toolbox genetic algorithm was used [15] to implement the GA. 1000 experiments are done for different numbers of tasks; each experiment uses a different set of task periods and execution times for the incoming and outgoing modes. These experiments are performed using 2 modes with task sets containing N = {2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128}, (

tasks for each experiment. Task utilization values are created using the UUniFast algorithm [16], with task periods randomly chosen from zero to 10 * N . Execution times are created by taking the product of the utilization and periods. Each initial set of N tasks is randomly divided into two modes with the same number of tasks, e.g. 32 tasks is two modes of 16 task sets in each mode. These two modes define the incoming I and outgoing O task sets. The periods of the incoming tasks can increase, reducing the interference with the outgoing tasks, thus making the system schedulable. The outgoing task parameters do not change. The mode transition deadline is implemented as a constraint in the genetic algorithm. This constraint is such that the outgoing tasks have to complete their last jobs before the mode time deadline, which is taken as 2 O e i . In these experiments the mode time multiplier, defined in the model section, is two. There are parameters that the GA has to use which are not mentioned due to lack of space. These parameters were tuned for the best performance of the GA. 'Tuning' the parameters, including initializing the population, is important for effective performance. The importance of these parameters are discussed at at MathWorks [15].

The population in the genetic algorithm was initialized randomly and close to the output of the scaleSA algorithm; 'close' means that the initial scale factors are between 1 and 10 and the initial worst case response times are plus or minus 30 from scaleSA. The scaleSA algorithm seems to be the next best algorithm for minimizing task set parameter changes.

In the first set of experiments, the utilization is fixed to 100 percent and the task periods are non-integer. This is due to the utilization constraint in BiniSA of ≤ 100 percent. In the second set of experiments, the utilization is 150 is percent. The task set parameters are integer; in general the integer or non-integer nature makes little difference in the comparison of the different algorithms, except it makes an unschedulable modes easier to generate at 100 percent utilization due to rounding and taking ceilings.

All of the information of the task sets, and output of the genetic algorithm of these algorithms is saved in files for statistical analysis. The statistics package R was used for the statistical analysis. Each of the algorithms generate different scale factors, and thus different fitnesses. In the case of the genetic algorithm there is a different scale factor for each for each incoming task. In the case of scaleSA the same scale factor is used for each task of the incoming mode, and the fitness is the scale factor times the number of tasks. BiniSA and TbTSA have different scale factors; in these two algorithms the scale factors are calculated by taking the ratio of the final to initial task period for each task.

Box plots of the distribution of the total fitness of the different task sets is shown in Figure 2. These box plots are for utilization of 100 percent of the combined two modes before the parameter changes, and for N = 32 and N = 64. The minimum total fitness is the sum of the scaling factors of half of these tasks since there are half in each mode, i.e. 16 and 32. The GA generally gives a lower total fitness than scaleSA or BiniSA. It does seem that at N = 32 there is little difference in the fitnesses of scaleSA versus scaleGA at utilization 100 percent, however there is a small difference in the mean and median. Also, in general, BiniSA has a larger spread of the total fitnesses in the distribution; this is due to increasing task periods from high priority to low priority.

In the first set of experiments the scaleGA and scaleSA gave similar results. This is due to the fact that the 2 modes have a total of 100 percent utilization. The incoming mode task parameters don't have to change too much to achieve schedulability of the mode transition. Box plots are also shown for the second set of experiments, in Figure 3. In these experiments, the total initial utilization was approximately 150, and the cases of N = 16, 32, 64 are shown. The GA had lower fitnesses on average for the 1000 task sets. BiniSA was not included because the utilization was greater than 100, and TbTSA was not included in the figure due to the large fitnesses that come from the TbTSA algorithm. The TbTSA algorithm produces large task changes and the results are instead included in the tables. TbTSA also in a non-negligible fraction of about 10 percent of the task sets does not produce a solution; this is possible because there could be an intermediate utilization of 100 percent of the partial task set even if the task period increases to infinity. This makes the comparison with the other algorithms more difficult. The GA fitnesses were less by 10 to 30 percent generally than all algorithms. The mean, median, and the inter-quartile ranges are shown in the box plots.

Histograms are presented of the second set of experiments in Figure 4. Note the distributions of the different algorithms. ScaleSA produces approximately normal distributions in the fitnesses, while scaleGA produces approximately Poisson distributions. This behavior of the histograms can be explained by the minimization. ScaleSA does not have a minimization goal of task set changes in the scaling of the task periods. scaleGA, and BiniSA, have minimization built into the algorithm (the latter of which is not used since utilization is greater than 100.) In all cases, the genetic algorithm produces, on average, lower fitnesses than scaleSA. Two tables, I and II, have the mean and median fitness values. Note that the median quantities are always smaller for scaleGA in the comparison of scaleSA and scaleGA. This is possibly due to both the fact that scaleGA is trying to minimize the task set changes and also that the distribution is Poisson-type.

There is an additional point that should be mentioned in the interpretation of the fitness function. The fitness function is the sum of the scale factors, not the sum of the period increases. The reason is that by using the scale factors, all the tasks are treated in a normalized fashion, as mentioned in the previous section.
The runtimes of the different algorithms are clear. The genetic algorithm scaleGA is the slowest because it searches for the optimal minimal task set changes with a population of chromosomes.

div.head: DISCUSSION
div.p: The scheduling problem of mode transitions is examined in this work by using a genetic algorithm. Mode transitions are formulated, examined, and made schedulable by changing task parameters such as periods. The total change in the task set is used as a fitness function, which is minimized in the GA algorithm. Unlike earlier techniques of sensitivity analysis, the task set is not changed task-by-task, but rather all at once.

In comparing with earlier sensitivity analysis', the GA formulation is seen to be more effective in minimizing the task set changes. This is a result of minimizing a fitness function of task set changes.

A clear generalization of this work is to examine more complicated mode transitions. This would mean including offsets, and more than 2 modes, different scheduling algorithms, abort points, for example.

An advantage of using the genetic algorithm in the sensitivity analysis of mode transitions is that multiple almost equivalent solutions to task set changes can be found. This is unlike the task-by-task earlier algorithms, and is a result of being able to examine all task set changes at once. This gives the real-time system designer more flexibility in designing systems.
